Definition: Does the government maintain a digital address register?
Comments: Kenya has a National Addressing System of Kenya (NASK) framework led by the Communications Authority, with policy/standards and plans to develop a national database and implement at county level, indicating under development rather than fully deployed registry.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The CA site and the National Addressing Policy (final draft, April 2023) were verified directly on the Communications Authority's own site; the original ict.go.ke PDF link timed out on fetch and could not be verified but its content is corroborated elsewhere. A Kenyan Parliament committee report (12 June 2026) confirms the National Addressing Bill 2025 remains at a 'green paper stage' pending public participation and second reading, with no operational national address database yet in place, corroborating and updating the existing score of 3 (Under development).
revised_comments: Kenya has a National Addressing Policy (finalised April 2023) and a National Addressing System of Kenya (NASK) framework led by the Communications Authority, but the enabling legislation remains in draft form. As of June 2026, the National Addressing Bill 2025 is undergoing parliamentary stakeholder consultation and is described by MPs as being at a 'green paper stage' ahead of public participation and second reading, with governance arrangements - including whether a standalone National Addressing Council is required - still contested between the Communications Authority, Council of Governors and national government departments. No national address database or fully operational digital address register has yet been established; implementation to date consists of policy development, a draft legal framework and county-level engagement, indicating the register remains under development rather than deployed.

Definition: Is the register integrated with the population register?
Comments: Civil registration data is captured into IPRS/National Population Register but UN CRVSID describes weak real-time updating mechanisms; hence partial integration between CRVS and population register.
revision_notes: Confirmed at 4. The UN CRVSID case study (Sept 2023) was re-read and confirms civil registration data feeds into IPRS/the population register but lacked robust real-time updating as of 2023. Fresher reporting was found and fetched: a Feb 2025 Biometric Update article states around 90% of birth certificate applications were digitised in 2024 with plans for automatic national ID issuance at 18 drawing on civil registry data via the Unique Personal Identifier (UPI); a May 2026 Biometric Update article confirms a digital birth e-notification pilot directly linking hospitals, Civil Registration Services and the Maisha Namba/UPI system, but this is only in phased rollout starting in Nairobi County as of mid-2026, not yet nationwide - consistent with 'partially integrated' rather than 'fully integrated'. The original 2018 World Bank ID4D diagnostic is dated and was not re-verified as it is superseded by the above.
revised_comments: Civil registration data in Kenya feeds into the population register (the Maisha Integrated Population Register, formerly IPRS) via the Unique Personal Identifier (UPI) assigned at birth, which later becomes the individual's national ID number at age 18. Since November 2023 a National Population Master Register has consolidated the UPI, Maisha Card and Digital ID into a single lifecycle identity system. A digital birth e-notification pilot launched in 2026 links hospitals directly to Civil Registration Services and the UPI generator, replacing manual birth notification and issuing a Maisha Namba immediately after delivery. Integration remains partial rather than complete: the e-notification system began as a Nairobi County pilot and is still being extended nationally, and legacy paper-based registration continues in many areas pending further legislative reform.

Definition: Is the population register integrated with the civil register?
Comments: UN CRVSID and World Bank ID4D note that civil registration data (birth/death records) feeds into IPRS but lacks effective real-time/automatic update mechanisms, implying partial rather than full integration.
revision_notes: Confirmed at 4 (mirrors reg-cr-pop, the inverse direction of the same integration). The UN CRVSID case study (Sept 2023) was re-read and confirms the linkage but with weak real-time mechanisms as of 2023. A Feb 2025 Biometric Update article and a May 2026 Biometric Update article describing a hospital-linked digital birth e-notification pilot feeding directly into the UPI/Maisha Namba population register were fetched and read; the pilot is in phased rollout from Nairobi County as of mid-2026 and not yet nationwide, supporting 'partially integrated' over 'fully integrated'. The original 2018 World Bank ID4D diagnostic is dated and was not re-verified as it is superseded by the above.
revised_comments: Kenya's population register (the Maisha Integrated Population Register, formerly IPRS) is updated from civil registration data via the Unique Personal Identifier (UPI), which is assigned at birth and later becomes the individual's national ID number at age 18. Since November 2023 the National Population Master Register has consolidated the UPI, Maisha Card and Digital ID into one lifecycle identity system. A digital birth e-notification pilot launched in 2026 links hospitals directly to Civil Registration Services and the UPI generator so that a Maisha Namba is issued immediately after delivery, replacing manual notification. This integration is partial rather than complete: the pilot began in Nairobi County and is still being extended to the rest of the country, and much of the population continues to be registered through legacy paper-based civil registration processes.

Definition: Are all non-citizens allowed to be included in the register?
Comments: Official IPRS/Maisha description states it provides comprehensive population data on all Kenyans and foreigners resident in Kenya; UN CRVSID case study notes registration systems include aliens and refugees, implying non-citizens can be included broadly.
revision_notes: Score of 4 retained but flagged for human review. The IPRS/Maisha site was re-fetched and confirms its stated vision is to hold comprehensive population data on 'all Kenyans and foreigners resident in Kenya', and formal identification pathways do exist for multiple non-citizen categories (Foreign National/Alien Certificates for permanent residents; Refugee IDs and asylum seeker passes issued by the Department of Refugee Services; Class M work permits for refugees under the Refugees Act 2021) - which supports 'All included' under the metadata's instruction to assess the broadest category formally eligible rather than actual registration rates. However, a detailed April 2025 report by Caribou Digital and the Robert Bosch Stiftung, 'Integration without Identification? ID System Challenges for Refugees and Migrants in Kenya', was fetched and read in full; it documents extensive practical barriers preventing refugees and migrants from obtaining paper and digital IDs, prolonged refugee status determination timelines, and a case of roughly 40,000 people wrongly excluded from citizenship/ID due to 'double registration' against the UNHCR database (a High Court ruling in 2025 began correcting this). Given the tension between formal eligibility (favouring 4) and substantial documented practical exclusion (favouring a lower score), this is marked for human review rather than asserted with confidence.
revised_comments: Kenya's population register (the Integrated Population Registration Service/Maisha Integrated Population Register) is formally intended to cover both citizens and foreign residents, with its stated mandate being to hold comprehensive population data on all Kenyans and foreigners resident in the country. Formal registration pathways exist for several non-citizen categories, including Foreign National/Alien Certificates for permanent residents, Refugee IDs and asylum seeker passes issued by the Department of Refugee Services, and Class M work permits for refugees under the Refugees Act 2021. In practice, however, research published in 2025 documents substantial barriers for refugees and migrants in obtaining these credentials, including prolonged refugee status determination processes, discrimination affecting border communities, and exclusion from digital ID and e-government platforms, such that practical inclusion lags behind formal eligibility.
